utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Mr. Registrar, can you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Jusic, you already know this, but I still have to remind you that you made a declaration at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth, and that you are still bound by that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good. Thank you very much. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General. We started out yesterday by putting a few questions to you regarding the El Mujahid detachment, and I think you answered thoroughly to those questions. My next question to you relates to the relationship or the relation between the 35th Brigade and the -- sorry, the 35th Division and the brigades. And I don't know if it is possible to bring back on the screen somehow, or maybe on the ELMO, the old organigramme that we were looking at yesterday, Exhibit 379, because I need to ask you a few questions about that once again. Right. I don't know if it is possible, Mr. Registrar, to have this organigramme displayed over the entire screen. Is that -- yes, excellent. Thank you very much. General, what is the relation between the 35 -- 35th Division, which we see on the top left corner of the screen, and the brigades, which are in the middle section of the right column? And to be more precise, which of the two are superior in terms of command?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relationship between the division command and brigade commands within that division is that of a subordinate and a superior. Therefore, the division command is a level of control which had the right to use as necessary all of its subordinate units. The units we can see in the left column are placed below the 35th Division, thus being directly subordinated to it. If I understood your question correctly, this would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then you may not have understood my question completely. But let us just stay with what you have just told us. In the left vertical column, we see the 35th Division on the top. And then we have a number of units, I believe, underneath. In the next box underneath, I see the 328th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And the one under that, the 329th Brigade. And then under that, the 351st or the 57th. I can't see -- 57th. I can't see.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be 351. 351.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And all the boxes below are all brigades; is that correct? Or maybe not the two bottom ones.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last two are not brigades. The third from the end and the fourth are. The 327th Maglaj Brigade. The last two are a Howitzer battery, as far as I can see, of 122-millimetre calibre, and the 35 engineering Company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excellent. So the picture we have here regarding the 35th Division is that it is a centre of command over a number of brigades and a Howitzer unit and engineering troops. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Then let's move to the right in the organigramme, because here I see that there's also something called the 303rd Brigade, the 314th Brigade and underneath that, the 330th, and so on. And in the bottom of that column, we have the El Mujahid detachment. And in the next column, I think it is the 7th Muslimanska Brigade. And under that one, we have a number of units, but I cannot see clearly what these units are. Now, my question is: What is the relation between the 35th Division and the 7th Muslim Brigade? It seems to me that the 35th Division would be a command that is superior to the 7th Muslim Brigade. But I'm not sure and I want you to clarify for me.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 35th Division was not superior to any units apart from those immediately below, below the box that reads "the 35th Division" in terms of establishment. The 37th Muslim [as interpreted], 303rd, et cetera, the -- in the part that you mentioned, those are independent brigades that were directly subordinated to the corps command. If necessary, I can explain the boxes that you cannot read. Below the 7th Muslim Brigade is the 3rd Light Artillery Battalion of anti-aircraft defence, then the 3rd Independent Engineering Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, sorry. Where is -- maybe you should have this on the ELMO so that you point what you're talking about, Mr. Witness. If somebody can help us please.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. I have to correct the transcript. Page 4, lines -- line 5, instead of the 7th Muslim Brigade as said, it reads "the 37th Muslim Brigade".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Vidovic. That's precisely why I'm beginning to ask that we be put on -- Okay. After the 37th -- after the 7th Muslim Brigade, you said 303rd. Now, I just want to know where you are, Witness, Mr. Jusic, which column you are on.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am now below the 7th Muslim Brigade. I think everything to the left has been cleared sufficiently. It is the 303rd -- well, let's start with the 303rd. The 303rd Chivalrous Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you point at it, please.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 303rd Chivalrous Mountain Brigade, here. [Marks]. The 314th Glorious Mountain Brigade, here. [Marks]. The 330th Light Mountain Brigade is here. [Marks]. The 319th Mountain Brigade is just below. [Marks]. And the El Mujahid Detachment. That is that in this column. Then in the next column, the same level of unit, there are the 7th Muslim Brigade, the 3rd Light Artillery Battalion of anti-aircraft defence, the 3rd Independent Engineering Battalion, independent engineering battalion. The 3rd logistics base, the 3rd Training Recruitment Centre Zenica, and the last one is garrison command. Those are the units. And in the last column, we have the battalion of the military police, the 3rd Tank Company, the 3rd Mixed Artillery Battalion, and the medical battalion. Those units were directly subordinated to the 3rd Corps command, and they are at a lower level than that of the division. We have two divisions here within a chain -- within a command and control briefing, we have the commander of the 35th Division, the commander of the 303rd, the commander of the 7th Muslim, and all the other brigades mentioned here that fall under the corps. They participate on equal footing at such briefings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now, the reason I'm putting these questions to you is that I think you mentioned yesterday during your testimony that the Vozuca action was organised or was -- was directed by the 35th Division. Did I understand you correctly? The -- the Vozuca -- the Vozuca pocket operation was liberated under the leadership of the 35th Division. But I may have misunderstood you and I just want to clarify.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday throughout -- I don't know about the interpretation and I don't speak English, but throughout I was saying that the planning and control of the Vozuca pocket operation, called Farz, was in the hands of the command of the 3rd Corps. In that operation, the 35th Division command was only one of the subordinate units to the command of the 3rd Corps. It received its task from the corps command the same as, for example, the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade. The 35th Division did not participate in the planning; however, once they were issued their task by the corps command, the 35th Division worked further on its task in detail so as to be able to forward that task to its subordinate units. It issued its subordinate units specific combat tasks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I think we should stop here in our exploration of the organisational structure of the 3rd Corps. My last line of questions to you relates to the possibility of prosecuting crimes committed by anyone within the 3rd Corps structure. Could you explain to us what -- first of all, what the normal procedure would be if a crime were committed by any member of the 3rd Corps; and then secondly, explain to us how these rules worked in practice; and finally, if you ever became aware of the prosecution of any crime committed by any member of the 3rd Corps. So let's start out by you briefly explaining what is the normal procedure to be followed if a crime is committed. Who takes action? Who does what? Briefly, if you can.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to be as brief as possible. The security service and the military police battalion were not subordinated to me in any way. What I can tell you is what I know about the procedure and nothing else. I can tell you the truth about the things I know, but I cannot testify that it is 100 per cent correct. If a member of the 3rd Corps committed a crime, the Military Police Battalion, or rather, its policemen, arrest such a person. The security organ, that is the department of the security of the corps headed by the chief of security, conducts an inquiry and questioning of the person suspected of having committed that crime. They gather evidence and witness statements, and if they have a basis to believe that indeed a crime was committed, it forwards that file to the court. As for the breaches of discipline or, rather, minor breaches, those things are resolved within the unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think we, because of the time, we shall have to concentrate on -- on major, more serious crimes. So you say that the military police would investigate the matter and bring it to the court. Would this be done within the 3rd Corps structure, or would it be done by military police under the ABiH as such? In other words, does the 3rd Corps have its own military police who would investigate a crime, and would it have it own lawyers to assess the responsibility of that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps had its military police, and those tasks were conducted by the military police of the battalion of the 3rd Corps. The main person in -- during an investigation is the security organ of the commander. Any prosecution or, rather, file submitted requesting prosecution, they have to be done by the commander. There is -- there was a lawyer who would go through the file, and on his advice the commander would then send the file to the county military court. The county military court, however, was not under the competence of the command of the 3rd Corps. Such courts were independent. I know that the then-president of the county military court was Mr. Adamovic. I believe he presides over a court in Sarajevo these days. He wouldn't have any sort of influence or intervention as regards his duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the lawyer who was attached to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the command, as one of the assistants of the commander, in particular in charge of legal affairs was Mr. Halilagic. I cannot recall his first name. I think it was Jusuf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Does Mr. Halilagic appear anywhere in this organigramme? Where would he fit in?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this organigramme shows the units of the 3rd Corps. It is not an organigramme of the corps command. During my testimony, we didn't use such an organigramme. Perhaps that is why some of the confusion ensued as to various -- the various assistants. He is within the corps command. It is an independent department for legal affairs. It is as independent as my staff was, for example. The two of us were at the same level. I was a colonel and he was a colonel. We were both within the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Excellent. So if we were to put him in, he would fit in somewhere in the top box, in the lower part of the top box where it says "3rd Korpus - Zenica," along with you and the other of the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is difficult to speak about that using this chart. The corps command had around 120 men, officers within it. One of them was I, then another person was he, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Let's just leave it. Because of the time constraints. My next question was: If you were aware of any prosecution being held against anyone -- any member of the 3rd Corps during your time as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't aware of that. I don't know of a single case. But they were not duty-bound to notify me, and I didn't find out any other way as to whether any proceedings took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So when you testified yesterday that you had not heard of any prosecution being held against any member of the 3rd Corps before, I think it was, 1994 or was it 1995, then that has to be seen in light of the fact that you would not be notified of any such prosecution; is that correct? In other words, there could have been prosecution -- prosecutions held without you knowing about it.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. It is possible. There was no duty on anyone's part to let me know, and I wasn't the one who would sit down and listen to stories very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And so the final question is: Did you ever hear of any legal action being taken against any member of the El Mujahid Detachment either before, during, or after your service as chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. This completes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I regret that I wasn't there yesterday, but I read the transcript of your testimony of yesterday. Now, there is one thing that I wanted to clarify with you regarding a question that was put by the Defence counsel, and the question was: "Can you agree that during 1992 and the first half of 1993 the Supreme Command did not control the situation in the field outside of Sarajevo?" And you answered that -- that you thought that there was no control of the situation. So first of all, I wanted to ask you whether this is something you think or -- or do you believe it is a fact that the Supreme Command did not control the situation? This is my first question.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this to be so at the time I was a commander and during that first year, nobody came to me to see firsthand what was the situation out on the ground, and neither could I on a single occasion establish contact with my superiors, and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much. Now, my next question is: What happened after the first half of 1993? Did the -- did the Supreme Command have control of the situation at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what to tell you. Well, I was not fully informed on what exactly happened or was happening, but I think there were some ways supported by UNPROFOR for certain members of the Republican headquarters or supreme -- well, first of all I have to clarify that the name of my superior commander changed. At that time it was the Republican TO, Main Staff, then Supreme Command. But at least as far as my superior command was concerned, I think that they found a way for members of that command to exit Sarajevo in an UNPROFOR vehicle and later on a tunnel was dug underneath the -- a strip of the Sarajevo airport. It was 1.5 metres high and 1.2 metres wide tunnel so that you can -- they could use it to enter and exit. As far as your question whether the commander could control the situation after that time, I believe that their capabilities were enhanced and the control was better, because part of the command of the General Staff managed to get out of the besieged Sarajevo and could control on the ground and issue tasks. I think that the situation improved after the first half of 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. One last question: And I'm referring back to the issue of the General Staff and the staff of the -- the staff and the General Staff. This is based off a question that Mrs. Vidovic put to you yesterday. And then the Presiding Judge asked you to clarify the difference between the staff and the General Staff. And the questions that were put by the Presiding Judge Moloto were very useful to clarify these issues, but I wanted to understand better. On the basis of your answer to the questions put by the Presiding Judge, can we conclude that the General Staff -- or rather - correction of the interpreter - the staff was subordinated to the General Staff, and then above all of this was a Supreme Command of the army? Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's partly correct. The staff was subordinated to the General Staff. It was a component part of the staff. Above the General Staff was only the Supreme Command, which is a Civilian Supreme Command. It was not a Military Supreme Command, which means the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was the exact structure: The staff, then the General Staff, and then the Supreme Command, which is the Civilian Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. So basically the Military Supreme Command, what was its name, then?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The supreme military command was the General Staff, but at different times it had different titles. They changed the name. But the General Staff prevailed for the longest time as a name. I'm afraid that you have not fully grasped what I tried to explain. If I may use two minutes to make a comparison. Let's take it that this Tribunal is the General Staff, this Tribunal at The Hague. It is comprised of -- so the Tribunal is comprised of some completely separate trials or groups of Judges who are in charge of different cases. It also is comprised of auxiliary services, guards -- I don't know the structure of this Tribunal. But the general label is "the Tribunal," as far as I know. This would be the General Staff. Courts are part of this highly esteemed body of the Tribunal. So the General Staff is a -- an umbrella under which we have the staff, logistics department, security department, morale department, intelligence department, et cetera, et cetera. So if I've managed to use the two minutes to improve your understanding of the General Staff and its structure, if I've done so, I'm very grateful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, thank you very much. It's perfectly clear now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, thank you very much. Sorry, Judge. Mr. Jusic, yesterday I heard you testify - and I'm checking whether I heard you correctly - that the El Mujahid Detachment was subordinated to the 3rd Corps, then resubordinated to the 35th Commission -- Division, rather, and then came back to the 3rd Corps. At some stage.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when the El Mujahid Detachment was originally under -- directly under the 3rd Corps, from when, to what date, and from when to when was it under the 35th Division, and from when to when was it back with the 3rd Corps? If you are able to.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot specify. As to make it my testimony, I can give you a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If you are able to give a rough estimate, please do.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly - and it can diverge from reality maybe by 15 days or one month - at the beginning of May, it was resubordinated to the 35th Division. May 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Wait. May I just interrupt you. Let's start with before it went to -- before it was resubordinated. When did it first come to the 3rd Corps for the very first time?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the El Mujahedin Detachment as a unit was established -- rather, work on its preparation was started in August 1993. When I say "work on its establishment," was work preparing for its establishment. Before it did not exist. There were groups which were not part of any system of command. So from August 1993, that detachment was established, and it was part of the 3rd Corps' composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it was part of the 3rd Corps from August 1993. I've just said: "So from August 1993, that detachment was established and it was part of the 3rd Corps' composition." Are you interpreted correctly?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From August. Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a brief period, maybe in October, it was resubordinated to the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group, out of which the 7th Corps grew. And I believe that in autumn 1993 it was resubordinated to the operational group of Bosnian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just -- let me just understand that. You said "for a brief period, maybe in October, it was resubordinated to the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group, out of which the 7th Corps grew." Now, do I understand you to say in October it became subordinated to the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you say -- now, was the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group a unit of any corps? And if so, which corps at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, operational groups, in terms of establishment, were precursors to corps or divisions. I correct myself. So instead of divisions, before divisions were established, we had the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group. I believe they were five in total, and divisions grew out of them. The 35th Division, before it was established, it used to be an operational group and its name was "Bosnia," which -- and this is within the composition of the 3rd group. And that operational group, the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group, was part of the 3rd Corps' composition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then from the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group in October 1993, what then became of the El Mujahid Detachment? How long did it stay under the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I cannot tell you precisely or out of my memory, because at that time I left the 3rd Corps' command to take my duty in Mostar in the 4th Corps, so I did not know for how long it remained in the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What you are saying is finally you are not able to estimate from the period when it was under the 3rd Corps, the period when it was under the 35th Division, and the period when it came back to the 3rd Corps. You're not able to answer that original question of mine. Because you went -- you went into these Bosnian Krajina operational groups, which I didn't know about, when I was -- that was my question, really. My question was the time.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, you asked me from the establishment of that detachment, and I started with the establishment of that detachment, trying to emphasise that two or three months down the road it was reconsolidated to the Bosnian Krajina Operational Group, and then it was returned to the composition of the 3rd Corps; and after that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was it returned? When was it returned to the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I cannot tell you, because I wasn't there. I was in Mostar. What I can tell you is that in 1995, that detachment was resubordinated to the 35th Division's command and that that resubordination lasted until the end of the Vozuca pocket operations, practically until the Dayton Accords. After the Dayton Accords, a decision was taken for that detachment to be disbanded, and it was disbanded in December 1995. When I say "disbanded," I mean that they were disarmed, had their equipment taken away from them, and that those troops were demobilised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Are you able to tell us when in 1995 it was subordinated -- resubordinated to the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I thought it was from May 1995 until November 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not -- I'm not 1 -- 100 per cent sure. This is roughly my estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, you say after the -- it was subordinated until the end of the Vozuca pocket operations, practically until the Dayton Accords. And you say after the Dayton Accords, it was disbanded. So it never went back to the 3rd Corps. Its life ended while it was under the 35th Division?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any degree of certainty. I cannot recall exactly, but I know that the corps command disbanded the El Mujahedin Detachment. But for it to be able to do so, it must have been returned to the composition of the 3rd Corps units. And in the disbandment of the 3rd -- of the El Mujahedin Detachment, the 35th Division's command had no role to play, so it was done by the 3rd Corps commander. But I don't know when that order was issued to return it to the 3rd Corps command. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me understand you. Are you saying the commander of the 3rd Corps cannot disband a unit under the 35th division unless he takes it out of the 35th Division and brings it back to the 3rd Corps before that disbandment?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, a commander may take a decision to -- for the 35th Division to effectuate the disbanding, but formally the El Mujahedin Detachment was part of the 3rd Corps. I know that nobody from the command of the 35th Division took part in it being disbanded. I don't know when the decision was written. It would be logical, in my mind, for that decision to be issued and for that detachment to be returned to the 3rd Corps. I did not see that decision. But everything was done by the personnel of the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that -- those answers, Mr. Jusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, both of you, for -- for -- actually not both, all three of you, standing up. Thank you. May we please move into private session. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Today when you were asked questions by Judge Harhoff, you indicated that you were not aware of any prosecutions because they were not duty-bound to inform you about prosecutions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were they duty-bound to inform somebody, some other person, some other superior about prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obligation that there was was to the corps commander and to the security organ of the Superior Command, or rather, the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the obligation was to inform the corps commander and the security organ of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did the security organ of the General Staff have a duty to report to anybody?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know that part of organisation, but as the corps commander had to report to his commander, the -- his superior commander had to report to his own commander. Of course, it was up to him to decide whether it was of significant importance so as to report. I don't know how things went in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Who is above the corps commander to whom the corps commander must report to?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the corps commander was the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. And now, was the security organ -- you said the security organ was part of the General Staff, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of any command, including the General Staff, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, who in the General Staff would the commander of the 3rd Corps report to?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through personal contact, he would report to the commander of the General Staff. In 1995, it was General Delic. It was an immediate contact. However, as the corps command, according to the General Staff orders, it sent reports to the operational centre of the General Staff and the operational centre was part of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And any -- and the corps commander would have been duty-bound to report to General Delic, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to explain the way things were. I'm trying to say the following: There were regular standard daily combat reports sent by the corps command, including the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me -- let me interrupt you. We're not talking about regular daily combat reports. We're talking about prosecutions. Criminal behaviour on the ground by units or members of the units. Let's -- let's stay focused on that one. Forget about daily reports. Who was duty -- what is the chain of reporting of criminal activity that happens on the ground and what are the obligations of each person right up to the top?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, please understand that I was chief of staff and not a commander. I don't know what the commander did personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you don't know, then say you don't know.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can talk in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just say you don't know if you don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is the case, then I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- if he reported anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I was asking you about the -- the duty, not whether anything did happen on the ground. What was the procedure? What was the requirement?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the procedure, as far as I know, was that it went through the security organ and the legal affairs, that is, the lawyer within the corps. That was the procedure that I know of. It should have been like that. As to whether it -- it actually was in place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's take a break, and we'll finish off when we come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a very final question, and I think this is a very simple one, just to confirm: Did I understand you clearly yesterday that you were saying - excuse me - that the 7th Chivalrous Muslim Liberation Brigade is the same thing as the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions. Yes, Mr. Mundis -- Mr. Wood. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I'd like to clarify a few things from your testimony in response to the Judges' questions, Mr. Jusic. In particular, you mentioned that the Mujahedin detachment never attended briefings where tasks were handed down. If the witness could be shown Exhibit 394, please. And I'll be asking about line 7 of that, which is on page 2 in both B/C/S and in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean line 7? Entry number 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, that is entry number 7, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we get page 2 of the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, do you see item -- or item 7 in the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And what does that indicate to you about what happened at 2100 hours at 09.09.1995?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It mentions a meeting of the corps commander with the El Mujahid Detachment commander. Other officers were not present. It was not one of the scheduled meetings. Therefore, I stand by the thing I said, which was that they never came to official meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: And just as a reminder, when did the battle begin, Operation Farz? When did Operation Farz begin to be executed?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operation Farz began on the 10th of September, 1995 at 6.00, a minute or two before or after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: If I could have page 4 in both English and B/C/S shown to the witness. Now, Mr. Jusic, yesterday you mentioned that the Mujahedin also would not submit reports. If I could draw your attention in particular to item 21.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: What does that indicate to you about the communication between the El Mujahid and the 3rd Corps commander at 6.34 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like that we show respect to each other in this courtroom. I never said that the El Mujahedin Detachment never reported on anything or anyone within the 3rd Corps command. The entry that we can see here in item 21 means that Ajman called, as is stated, the commander. It was a conversation done via certain communication means, and he reported that the El Mujahid Detachment seized the facilities of Paljenik and Ravno Polje. I commented on this document before when

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: simply made use of the possibility he had, that is, to use the communication links to boast to the commander. He went -- he bypassed the regular command and control chain, and he bypassed the division commander. Technically speaking, he could have done this, and he did. This is a conversation that took place. It was not a document in which he reports on anything. He simply called him by telephone, I believe, and it was merely a conversation. I don't think it falls under the topic of reporting and the system of reporting that was in place. They were completely out of it.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Where -- I want to follow up a little bit on what you just said. If you could tell the Trial Chamber, where was the 3rd Corps commander when he received this report?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the question to be imprecise. The 3rd Corps commander was at the observation post of the 35th Division commander at the Klek facility. He went there, and he was supposed to be there. I suppose he was.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Where --

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he could have gone anywhere. In any case, he was supposed to be there. I'm trying to say that I was never sure where he was, and it was not in my competence to observe his movements. Perhaps he would tell me that he would be there, and then I could reach him there. Whether he was closer or further afield at that time, I don't know, but according to this, he was supposed to have been at the observation post at Klek.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Where was the 35th Division commander during the beginning of the execution of Operation Farz?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know exactly. I think he was at the observation post as well.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: If I could have page 5 shown to the witness, and in particular, if attention could be drawn to line -- item 25. Mr. Jusic, what does this indicate to you about the reporting between the El Mujahid Detachment and the 3rd Corps commander?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this was another call via a communication device whereby he orally informed the commander on how far they managed to reach.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: If you could please look at item 28 on that same page. And, for the record, that is page 6 in the English. Oh, I withdraw that. Item 28 is -- is also on page 5 in the English. Again, sir, what does this indicate to you about the communications between the El Mujahid Detachment and other units on that day?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether my role here is that of an expert. I believe to be a simple witness. I can see what it says here, and this is the first time that I see it. Provided this is true, it would seem that the El Mujahedin Detachment requested that the Stog facility be engaged, which was transferred to the chief of staff at elevation or observation post 923. Therefore, he requested - we don't know who - to do something. We only have Sivro's signature. This was the person who made the entry. However, it doesn't state who the detachment commander requested to talk to. I can only tell you what it says here: Activities during the combat operation whereby the given unit requested artillery support and, I presume, the commander approved.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: If you could also tell the Court what -- what is meant by the letters "NS." Who is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "chief of staff." "NS" is short for chief of staff. If I connect that with the rest of the sentence, it was probably me, since I was at elevation 923.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I'd like to ask a question of the witness based on an answer he gave in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Your Honour, without conceding the point that documents can be shown to the witness in response to questions that were put to Your Honours, the -- or by Your Honours to the witness, the Prosecution is prepared to move on at this point. Oh, one moment. On that point, Your Honour, though, I do want to -- the next point that I was going to get to would include the introduction of a document, but I believe this document would help to clear up a lot of confusion around a certain aspect of the case that has come up during the examination; that is, the questions put to the witness by the Court. With Your Honours' indulgence, I would like to show just one last document to the witness. I think it will be helpful to the Trial Chamber and to -- to the record. And for the record, that is document P02133.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in preparation.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, what is the effect from a military standpoint of this order that is written on -- in this document?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I have to reiterate, this is the notion of resubordination, as I've already said, which means that the corps command resubordinates of the -- resubordinates the El Mujahedin Detachment to the 35th Division and that they asked to be used, according to the 35th Division's plans, with a view of achieving the task that the commander may give to them. Some tasks have been listed here, but to resubordinate is a term in our military terminology which denoted forwarding physically, in physical terms, and formally, a unit into the composition of another unit - in this case, the 35th Division - which then has the right and competence to command them and the duty to supply them, in terms of logistics, security, et cetera, as in the case of all other units which are formally part of its composition. This was -- would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The Prosecution moves that this be tendered into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is tendered into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 396.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, you mentioned earlier today on page 12, lines 1 through 3, that once the tunnel was built beneath the airstrip in Sarajevo it was easier for commanders to leave Sarajevo, and the command and control improved after that. In relation to that, sir, when you were in the 3rd Corps, did you see Rasim Delic there?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that the first year of the war passed that I never saw anybody from the General Staff. Later on I did see him when he assumed his duty, and I did see him at the command of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: How often was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to tell you how often, but given that I was for a part -- for a time head of artillery, my office was along the corridor that he had to take to reach to the commander's office, so it seemed to me that this was often, but I cannot tell you how often. On a monthly basis, maybe one, two, or three times a month. But since I had not seen my superior officer for a year before that, it seemed to me much more often than before.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And during what period was this that you would see him on a monthly basis maybe one, two, three times a month?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period while I was head of artillery. June 1993 to approximately April -- March 1994. Over six or seven months.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: What about during the period of time when you were the 3rd Corps chief of staff? How often would you see him in the 3rd Corps command?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to see him less often during that period of time. I could not say how often, but far less often. It seemed to me that two months would pass without me seeing him. I understand why he used to come more often during that period. As I understood it, it was he was fresh in the duty and I would have done the same, meet as many units as possible to assess the situation and try to influence the battle readiness of such units and improve C and C, control and command.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, do you remember giving a statement to an OTP investigator in 2006, in November -- in September?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PROSECUTOR
utterances.text: And do you remember, sir, what it is that you said in that statement, about how often Rasim Delic was in the 3rd Corps command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. The Prosecutor has now obviously engaged in cross-examination of his own witness, and I have not heard you, the Bench, allowing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not engaging in cross-examination of this witness. In fact, what I'm doing is laying the foundation to refresh his recollection about something that he said about this earlier. And if -- if you see the line of my questioning, that is where I'm headed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but, you know, one -- let me tell you, Mr. Wood, once you start referring to the witness's statement, and you saw I turned to Judge Lattanzi, you -- you've given us the impression that you're now trying to impeach your own witness. Now, I think if you have to remind him of something, you can remind him without necessarily going to the statement. You know, and obviously when you try to impeach your witness, you're beginning to try and cross-examining, just like Judge -- I beg your pardon, Madam Vidovic is suggesting. I don't know what the question is you are going to ask, and I would like to hear the question before I rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The question at this time is: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was, yeah: Do you recall making a statement to the investigator? But I don't know what the question is in the statement that you're going to put.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Do you recall what it is you said to the OTP investigator in September 2006?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure he gave him a statement. He said a lot of things to the investigator on that date. But then you've got to be able to say exactly what is it you're talking about at this point that he said about the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. And I can even provide him a copy of that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that's not the point. We want to find out what the purpose of this questioning is. That's why I said, what is it -- what is it in that statement you want to refresh his memory about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: About the issue how often he saw the 3rd -- Rasim Delic in the 3rd Corps command during his time as chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But -- yes, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Prosecutor, all of this is very interesting, but it would have been very interesting if you had put all these questions during your examination-in-chief. It seems like you are resuming another examination-in-chief. And I can understand that when you're putting questions referring to strictly what the Bench put as questions. But now you're referring to preliminary statements made to the investigators. These are questions you should have put during your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] To add to that, I just want to say this question of the tunnel, did it arise from the Bench's questions or did it arise from your opposite member's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe it arose from Your Honours' questions in -- I don't have the page in front of me, but I believe it was about -- Judge Lattanzi had asked about the command and control early in the war, in 1992. The witness answered that things did improve once the tunnel was built and the commanders could get out into the field and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But Judge Lattanzi was asking about what was said yesterday, because she read that in the transcript of yesterday's.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it -- the first time it arose was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. Now -- and now you're trying to clarify anything that Judge Lattanzi -- what is it that Judge Lattanzi asked today that needs clarification about the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It's -- it's more about -- not so much about the tunnel, Your Honour, as about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: About --

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The command and control and how things improved afterward, after things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: After the tunnel was built.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the relevance of the tunnel, yes. But what is so unclear from what Judge Lattanzi asked that needs clarification on the frequency of meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: I believe it adds context, Your Honour, and it's a question that will help the record, if we can determine how often -- following up on that question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but what was unclear in what Judge Lattanzi asked? You're not answering my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: It adds further context to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, what was unclear? I'm not asking what it adds. What was unclear about Judge Lattanzi's questions and the answers thereto?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: The time period, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The time period?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why don't you ask him about the time period, rather than refer him to a statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Well, I've done that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, why do you need the statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but regarding the question of the time period, the witness answered my question in a very precise manner. He confirmed the period of time concerned. During the cross-examination, he said from 1992 until the first half of 1993. So my question referred to what happened later on regarding the command and control after the first half of 1993, that is. And he answered very clearly. He referred specifically to this second period of time. So I fail to see the need to come back on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think -- I think we need to rule on the objection. The objection is upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The Prosecution has nothing further from this witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any questions arising, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, a few.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Mr. Jusic, I wanted to ask you about our discussion about communication links between the corps command and the El Mujahid Detachment. Do you agree that the operations' logs are something that is not -- is not considered regular reports?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I explained that yesterday during my testimony. I explained what the importance of operations logs was and what their purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore reports are regular reports from one command to its superior command; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the standard way of reporting, and they should have encompassed everything that the given command meant to report to its superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Only the things entered in such regular or interim reports represents the regular line of reporting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the counsel please pause between question and answer and repeat her last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Madam Vidovic? Could you please pause between question and answer and could you please repeat the last question. That's the interpreter asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: If something was not made part of a regular or interim combat report sent to a superior command, then one can take no position regarding that issue and no decision can be expected from the superior command on the issue. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now to turn to Their Honours' questions today that had to do with submitting criminal reports and prosecutions. Mr. Jusic, is it correct that you did not work for the security department and you did not receive their reports?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that processing operational information gained in the field, conducting investigations, and submitting criminal reports is a procedure that is fully regulated by the regulations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it was so in the war?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as regards the processing of crimes and the perpetrators thereof, of the people who committed criminal offences, there is nothing in particular that I can tell you about. Occasionally I even consider whether to talk about it at all. Since I can only provide my opinion, my assumption, which may not reflect the truth, I would prefer far better that these questions be asked of someone else. All I know is that there was a security organ and the military police and that their competence included preventing committing criminal offences. There is also a legal affairs organ that had to do with the same thing. If I may add another sentence: Security organs were not well-liked by the commands. Occasionally, it even occurred to me, as chief of staff, that they would control and monitor me in my private life. Therefore, I never wanted to establish any contact with those people in case they didn't want to tell me something.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: I know you didn't work in that field, but do you agree that there were rules for the military police?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Rules for the military security?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force during the wartime in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it clearly prescribed who it was that submits a criminal report to the military and county prosecutor. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that such a thing was in existence, although it was not a part of my job. I never read that particular law on the competencies regarding criminal reports. All I know is that the organs I enumerated were supposed to deal with such issues, and it was usually dealt with at the level of units.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that there was a Law on Criminal Procedure in Bosnia during the war?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: His Honour asked you whether you know of a single criminal report being submitted or prosecutions established, and you've answered to that. During the time when the corps was formed and in the next one year's time, over 800 criminal reports were submitted for different offences.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a piece of information I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you do not exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not. After the war, I learned that there was a plan of activity of security organs in order to establish the existence of criminal acts committed by foreign members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I learned after the war that such a thing existed and that the General Staff conducted such activity. However, during the war I didn't know of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to go back to the chart that you were asked about by Their Honours. I believe it is Exhibit 379. 379. Please have a look at it. You testified extensively on this chart and today as well. Did I understand correctly that this chart of the 3rd Corps is incorrect in one of its parts?

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday, and my memory serves me quite well in that regard. I know what the chart looked like, and in principle this was not the correct chart of the 3rd Corps as regards its subordinate divisions. I can go even further and say that 351st Liberation Brigade in the first column under "the 35th Division" was never formed. I'm trying to say that there are incorrections in this chart; however, the rest is true. But it -- the way it's shown here is that if the 3rd Corps commanded at the same footing to the 35th Division and to the 328th Division. It was the other way around; the 35th Division commanded directly to the 328th Brigade. Therefore the line above should have been interrupted in the part which goes from the 35th Division to the 328th.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusic, thank you. Just to clarify for the Court. Charts as this one, in principle, can change. If one looks at this one, one should be able to establish the time period it reflects, since units were being moved in the field.

utterances.speaker: KADIR JUSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only were they being moved but there was constant reorganisation of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its subordinated units, starting with the General Staff, which changed in terms of its composition. I understand that because of the function I carried, we were simply looking to come up with better solutions for the organising of the army and its subordinate units. That year, in 1995, the manoeuvre battalions were organised instead of the 351st Liberation Brigade in Zavidovici. In its stead, the 5th Manoeuvre Battalion Brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have another question, Your Honours, or maybe a couple that should be dealt with in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, this brings us to the end of your testimony, Mr. Jusic. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, may I thank you for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may stand down. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you for your patience. After all, I am a person of 60 years of age, you know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that all? Only 60? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess this is a convenient point. Okay. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I may, I'd like to record something on the record, with -- with the leave of the Bench. Essentially it concerns the way that the Office of the Prosecution have dealt with the examination-in-chief of this witness. At the outset, can I say that the Defence was heartened by the comments of the Bench, and in particular what Judge Lattanzi had to say, where she stated in connection with the questions that arose from the Prosecution arising out of the Judges' questions that these are questions that should have been asked during examination-in-chief. The Defence's position is that the Prosecution have a positive duty when examining a witness in chief to lead evidence relating to the charges contained in the indictment. We know that the indictment alleges that General Delic had command and effective control over the 3rd Corps and units subordinate to the 3rd Corps. During the examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, in my submission, asked no real questions as to this ultimate issue. They also, in my submission, failed to ask any questions that went towards gathering any evidence that might show an indicia of effective control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the purpose of this address?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's just to record our concerns. I'll make it brief, if I may, and then -- if you don't understand me or if you have any follow-up questions, I'd be very happy to -- to deal with it. But in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I -- I'll tell you why I asking you the question. I do understand that you may have concerns, and get me right, you are perfectly entitled to putting your concerns on the table if they have to be put on the table. But I'm yet to come across any lawyer who does everything by the book and never makes a mistake, and if they make a mistake, I don't think it is for the Defence to give them a lecture on how to conduct their case, particularly here in court. If they make a mistake that prejudices the Defence, the Defence is entitled at that point to stand up and object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is exactly the issue. We say that a matter has arisen today which prejudices the Defence. And bearing in mind the witnesses that we are to -- the Trial Chamber is going to hear from in the near future, a similar situation could arise in respect of those witnesses, and that is the reason for putting on the record our concerns now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But when --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That situation arises, it is expected of the Defence to jump up and object. What concerns me is that you -- you tend to be giving the Prosecution a lecture on how to conduct their case. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that is an apposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I suppose what we're doing is we're laying down a marker now so that not only the Trial Chamber is aware but also the Prosecution is aware of -- of our concerns so that next time, if a similar situation arises, we will be on our feet; we will be objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but you don't have to make a mark for that. You've just got to be on your feet every time that situation arises without having made a mark. It is your right at every turn to stand up and object.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Your Honour, I believe it is the right of the Defence to also draw to the Trial Chamber's attention matters of concern so it can be recorded, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, is it your concern -- is it a matter of concern to you that, according to you, the Prosecution has not presented its case as it ought to have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That they didn't mention any indicias that you were referring to and in that case in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is of personal concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously if they don't mention that, according to you, isn't it for you to argue at the end of the case that they didn't present their case for you to meet and therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we would say is by taking this approach, and whether it's a conscious approach or an unconscious approach by the Prosecution, we would say that it is giving rise to unfairness to the Defence. Perhaps if I can just briefly explain the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And this is it: Having put a succinct number of questions in examination-in-chief, the Defence dealt with -- it cross-examined the witness based on those questions, focusing on those succinct issues raised. We would submit that the Bench was somewhat puzzled by the evidence of this witness. He is a chief of staff of the 3rd Corps, obviously someone in a high-ranking position and in a situation that he potentially was aware of -- of many facts. Now, we would submit that because of that, the Defence -- the Trial Chamber was placed in a situation where it asked a lot of questions of clarification. They lasted a long time. Some of those questions touched upon ultimate issues in this case. Some of questions were put in a robust manner. Now, the upshot of that was that that opened the door for the Prosecution to come back and present a whole host of evidence that, in our submission, should have been raised, if they wanted to raise it, during the examination-in-chief. Secondly, because the Prosecution were able to raise these issues in subsequent -- consequence of your questions, the Defence lost the opportunity to cross-examine the Prosecution on matters arising out of those questions. And really that's -- that's the nub of my submission. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And so in essence, Your Honour -- I don't want to say much more about this, but in essence it would appear to us that the Prosecution could or has gained a tactical advantage by holding back an examination-in-chief and waiting for the -- the Trial Chamber to put a lot of clarifying questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hold no brief for the Prosecution, and I see your opposite member is on his feet. But before he gets on his feet, I just want to get some clarification from you. One, I don't know how the Prosecution knows what questions the Bench is going to ask to enable them to withhold certain questions only to put them after the Bench's questions, because the Bench could say, "We have no questions." That's the one thing. The other point that -- or the other message that I'm getting coming from that last statement you are making, that the Prosecution gains a tactical advantage by the questions from the Bench, I'm not quite sure whether the underlying message is you, the Bench, stop asking questions because you're giving these guys a tactical advantage or not, because -- you know, the Bench can ask any question it wants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If I may be clear, Your Honour. I'm not putting that -- I'm not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not suggesting that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: No, as I've said, the nub is that we lose the chance to cross-examine on the answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you have the chance to cross-examine the witness after the questions by the Bench. And if there's anything that the Bench raised that is -- that was misplaced by the Bench because the Bench doesn't understand which way the things are going, you have the opportunity to clear them up with the witness. And that's why counsel have the opportunity to ask questions after the Bench has asked questions. Is it absolutely correct then to say that you lose the opportunity to -- to cross-examine the witness? Particularly because you ask your questions after the Prosecution has asked its questions arising from the Bench, the Bench's questions. So you do have the last word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the normal course of events, you're right, it wouldn't be a problem. Fairness would flow from that. But in this situation, where, in our submission, the Prosecution has held back with important questions and documents and then the questions of the Bench have opened up a number of issues which has led to the Prosecution introducing a whole host of documents that, in our submission, should have been introduced at the outset, then we have lost the chance really to -- to hone in on those documents and those issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you -- but you objected, and in this particular instance the Bench upheld your objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the Bench did uphold the objection. As I've said at the outset, we were heartened by that. But we did -- the objection pertained to only a number of documents that were raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought you said you were heartened by the comments of Judge Lattanzi, not the -- not the upholding of the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, both, Your Honour. It was ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. What relief are you seeking from the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't know whether you -- you're in the position to order any relief. But what I would like the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution to be aware of is that if in the future with similar witnesses a similar situation arises, we will be putting forward a robust objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: -- whenever appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I want to believe that you have been putting up a robust objection and a robust defence up to now, that you are not only going to start from today. Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis, you had something to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I do indeed, Your Honours, but I do note the time. We are past the normal point where we would break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With all due respect, if we could take a break commencing now, take perhaps a 30-minute break, I would like to respond in, not great detail, but certainly more than just a few moments to the comments made by my learned colleague. I would -- I would respectfully ask that we resume at 6.00 so that I could be afforded a -- an opportunity to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll then resume at 6.00 and come back. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. I will be brief, in light of the hour of the day. But I do want to make just a few points in response to the comments made by my learned colleague Mr. Robson. The first -- the first issue, Your Honours, is -- and I completely acknowledge the fact that the Presiding Judge earlier this afternoon in the transcript clearly indicated that if a mistake was -- if a mistake was made - and this was at line -- lines 20 to 22 of page 57, where the Presiding Judge said, "I've yet to come across any lawyer who does everything by the book and never makes a mistake - I want to be very clear on behalf of the Prosecution team that I lead that, in our respectful submission, no mistake was made. And I clearly acknowledge that Your Honour said "if a mistake was made." But I want -- I want to put on the record the position that we take, that no mistake was in fact made, simply to clear that issue as far as we're concerned. With respect to the issue of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say I wasn't suggest a mistake was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm not suggesting the opposite either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand that, Your Honour. And I appreciate that. Let me -- let me go to the -- the broader issue that the Defence raised, which goes to the way and means by which this Prosecution team is leading the evidence in this case. I would agree with comments made by the Presiding Judge. It is clearly within the purview of the Prosecution as to how we go about proving our case. I take issue with one thing my learned colleague Mr. Robson said, again reflected on page 57, lines 5 through 8, where the Defence submitted that the Prosecution asked no real questions going to the ultimate issue. I have said this before, and undoubtedly I will say it again in this case, this case is largely a circumstantial case. It requires a number of witnesses, each of whom will present one or perhaps two pieces of a very large puzzle. If I were in a position to call one witness who could testify about each and every aspect of this case, I would do that. Unfortunately, we're not in a position to do that, and so we need to call a number of witnesses, each of whom will provide the Trial Chamber with evidence on what that individual witness knows about the issues relevant to this case. Perhaps the witness who just testified had very little to say going to the ultimate issues to be resolved. Perhaps his evidence was of more significance. That's an issue for the Trial Chamber to decide once they've heard all of the evidence. And so I do take objection to a submission that each and every witness will have 100 per cent evidence on the ultimate issue in the case that. Is simply not the way large cases of this type unfold before the Trial Chamber. This does, however, raise a broader question or a broader issue, which, again, I'm sure that if we get to the phase where there's a Defence case following the 98 bis submissions, the Defence very well might be in the same or a similar situation that the Prosecution is in. All cases heard before the International Tribunal - and this case is not an exception - face time restraints and resource restraints due to a number of factors beyond each and every one of our control. Those factors relate to time available primarily, and the issue that -- that we are facing and will face, as this case progresses, is very simple: We have time limits and we understand those and we accept those. Within those time limits, however, it may not be possible for us to present all of the evidence of a given -- that a given witness may have to offer. And as a result of that, decisions have to be taken as to whether to question a witness on a particular issue or not. Quite often we make a decision - sometimes at the -- at the very last moment, given time constraints - that another witness who's scheduled to appear in the future might be a better witness than the current witness, and as a result of that we forego asking questions on certain issues due to time constraints. Similarly, as Your Honours are well aware, as everyone in this courtroom is well aware, the Prosecution exhibit list has more than 2000 exhibits on it. My team is undertaking efforts to identify what we've -- what we are calling core exhibits, that is the most crucial documents or videos or photos or other evidence that must be put before the Trial Chamber before we can close our case. Of these 2000 exhibits on our list, there are approximately 400 exhibits that have been admitted into evidence, probably slightly more than half of which have been tendered by the Defence; meaning that at this stage of the proceedings, the Prosecution has tendered into evidence approximately 10 per cent of the exhibits that are on our exhibit list.
